narrative: The model estimates your probability of failing the final year at 13.0%, meaning failure is not the most likely outcome but is still a real risk; the remedial requirement is a precaution to stop that risk from growing. The strongest factor in your assessment is your record of no past class failures, which lowers your risk and pushed the decision toward passing. The second strongest factor is your intention to continue to higher education, which also works in your favor; among students who passed, all wanted higher education. The main factor raising your risk is weekly study time. You report studying under two hours, whereas most passing students study two to five hours, and only about one in five passing students study less than two hours. So the warning is not driven by a history of failure or low ambition; it is driven by study habits that leave too little margin. To improve, use the remedial courses to build a regular schedule of at least two to five hours of study each week, lean on the family support you already have, and ask for help early when a subject becomes difficult. With no past failures and a clear higher-education goal, small changes in study time can substantially reduce the remaining risk.
